articles.title_orig: House Republicans consider issuing subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - ABC News
articles.title_zh: House Republicans consider issuing subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Several House Republicans called for a closed-door briefing.
The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Brian Mast, told ABC News on Tuesday that he's prepared to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond by Wednesday to a request from several House Republicans for a closed-door briefing on Huang's reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Last week, Mast as well as Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and John Moolenaar, the chair of the House China Committee, sent Huang a letter requesting he appear for a "joint, closed-door briefing."
The focus of the briefing would be on Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" after the tech giant on Sunday announced an investigation into its CEO following New York Times' reporting that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed.
Jensen Huang has not yet responded to the Republicans' request that he appear for a briefing. Asked by ABC News if he would consider issuing a subpoena to Huang should he not respond, Mast said "absolutely."
It's unclear how a potential subpoena of Huang would play out. House Republicans lose control of their committees in January when the chamber turns over to Democrats. The subpoena would likely expire and Democrats would need to issue a new one.
ABC News reached out to Nvidia for comment from Huang for this story.
Congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China also sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang. It is not known if Huang will appear before that committee; Nvidia hasn't publicly responded to the request.
Mast said there is a "lengthy" list of things he wants to hear from the Nvidia CEO including what correspondence he had with the Chinese government. Mast added that he is "100%" worried about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he runs the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"They're American chips. You know. So we thank God that Jensen is an American entrepreneur. You know, it's an American tech company because they're the best chips anywhere in the globe," Mast said. "But that being said, we don't want China to access them, to use them, to produce them like that."
Nvidia's board said they have "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised" by Huang's affair.
Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement further said.
Several Democrats have expressed concerns about national security after the report, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling ABC News that there are "real concerns" that need to be addressed.
"We're going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of America's national security," Jeffries said.
On Monday, President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the matter. Trump said he spoke with Huang in a phone call on Monday, during which the CEO said that he "didn't know" he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," the president told reporters during a press briefing on Monday.
It's unclear when -- if ever -- the Trump administration alerted Nvidia that its CEO was the target of an alleged Chinese espionage plot.
The Chinese government has denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment about the New York Times story on the relationship.

articles.title_orig: Stanley Zabar Has Died. He Managed the Books, and the Slaw, at a N.Y.C. Landmark.
articles.title_zh: Stanley Zabar Has Died. He Managed the Books, and the Slaw, at a N.Y.C. Landmark.
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- Stanley Zabar, the co-owner of the iconic Upper West Side gourmet grocery store Zabar's, has died at the age of 94, according to a statement posted on the store's Instagram page .
The statement described Zabar as a "quiet force behind our family business," with Stanley having "spent decades working with his brother Saul to build upon and carry forward the vision of their parents, Louis and Lillian Zabar."
Zabar's legal and financial acumen was described as "vital" in shaping the Zabar's into a beloved New York City institution, that was first founded by his parents in 1934.
The Upper West Side shop is known for its fancy cheese, smoked fish, and coffee among other specialty items.
Over time, five locations were consolidated into a large single market at West 80th and Broadway.
Stanley's death comes just over a year after his older brother Saul died at the age of 97.

articles.title_orig: Gas prices fall below $4 a gallon for first time since July
articles.title_zh: Gas prices fall below $4 a gallon for first time since July
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Oil and Gas Association President Tim Stewart discusses the potential impact of Democratic energy policies on the Texas oil industry. Stewart weighs in on proposed gas tax suspensions and regulatory shifts.
Gasoline prices fell to their lowest level since July on Tuesday, with the national average price slipping below $4 a gallon for the first time in months.
Data from AAA showed that the national average price dropped about 3 cents per gallon from Monday's report, with the average slipping to $3.97 a gallon on Tuesday.
Gas prices have fallen about 17 cents per gallon over the last week, and roughly 39 cents from a month ago, according to AAA's data.
CONSUMER INFLATION RISES FASTER THAN EXPECTED IN OCTOBER, CPI REPORT SHOWS
Gas prices remain volatile and reached their lowest level since July on Tuesday, according to AAA data. (M. Scott Brauer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The decline in prices comes as refiners have switched to winter blends of gasoline that typically cost slightly less than summer blends, which can be sold at gas stations starting as early as mid-September.
Winter weather tends to result in fewer drivers on the road, which can reduce demand for fuel and contribute to a downward trend in prices, and AAA noted that gas prices may fall between 10 and 30 cents per gallon during the winter months.
TRUMP ADMIN POURING $480M LOAN INTO GULF OF AMERICA OIL AND GAS PROJECT
Refineries have switched to winter blends of gasoline that tend to be slightly cheaper than summer blends. (Sharon Steinmann/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Consumers have faced higher gas prices for much of this year during the war in Iran, which has disrupted the flow of oil from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz and, in turn, constrained supplies for refiners to convert crude into gasoline.
Gas prices hit a recent peak at $4.50 a gallon May 11, 2026, then declined to a recent low of $3.77 a gallon on July 6, according to data from the Energy Information Administration .
CEO WARNS HIGH DIESEL PRICES COULD TRIGGER A 'VICIOUS CYCLE' OF SURGING FOOD PRICES
The Iran war has disrupted the flow of oil from the Middle East to global markets, pushing prices higher. (Giuseppe Cacace/AFP via Getty Images)
Ongoing tensions in the Middle East contributed to a rise in gas prices as summer turned to fall, with the national average reaching $4.47 a gallon on Sept. 21, 2026.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics on Tuesday released the October consumer price index, which showed gasoline prices were up 1% last month, a much slower rise that followed monthly jumps of 9.1% in September and 3.9% in August.

articles.title_orig: British comedian and children’s author David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct
articles.title_zh: British comedian and children’s author David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct
articles.content_orig:
TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams and the rape conviction of Russell Brand.
In a statement, Ross said he was once "on friendly terms with both men", but that at the time he was "genuinely unaware of their conduct".
ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. Walliams denies all the allegations against him. Brand was sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape on Monday.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said that the allegations against Walliams were the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the media.
Ross said he was "as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation".
He added: "My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."
Jonathan Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.
In the ITV documentary revealing the allegations, Ross is pictured at an event also attended by a woman who later made accusations about the conduct of Walliams.
In his statement, Ross also addressed a joke he made at a comedy awards show in 2004, in which the punchline suggested Walliams would be "going home" with a 15-year-old.
Ross acknowledged the controversial quip and described it as "tasteless".
He added: "This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script writing team and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect.
"Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him.
"I also like to think that I would have acted upon that knowledge."
Ross and Brand were also widely criticised for leaving lewd voicemails for Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs, the grandfather of Georgina Baillie with whom Brand was in a consensual relationship in the mid-2000s, during a BBC Radio 2 broadcast.
Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years imprisonment for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and the Metropolitan Police has confirmed several people have approached them about the disgraced star since his conviction.
Walliams rose to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent, and launched a best-selling series of children's books.
Several women have spoken to the Guardian and ITV News as part of a joint three-year investigation by the media companies, accusing Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. The investigation was published after Walliams lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.
One of the women now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15-years- old as a "sexual assault".
Walliams denies the allegations, and in a statement to journalist shared by the Guardian said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
He acknowledged that "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".
The Metropolitan Police have since contacted the Guardian and ITV News "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".
Comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News on Tuesday that she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations raised with her about Walliams.
A young TV worker had approached Beaumont about concerns of Walliams engaging inappropriate behaviour with "young girls" who were "definitely" older than 16, the comedian said.
The young person said he had worked on a program involving Walliams where he was tasked with taking the "young girls" to Walliams' dressing room, adding: "He felt they were vulnerable".
"At the time, he didn't think there was a process, a way to let people know within the TV company what was happening and how he felt and I was really worried."
Beaumont said she reached out to an alleged victim who was "in a really bad way" and was worried about her well-being but said the woman "declined my offer of support".
The 43-year-old comedian said she had never worked with Walliams or witnessed any inappropriate behaviour from him but was "worried that these girls were very young".
She believes there is not a robust "duty of care" to protect people within the TV industry from sexual misconduct and an adequate reporting system for whistleblowers.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Tuesday: "These allegations are the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power in an industry where we have known for so long that the power imbalances are huge.
"Russell Brand's eventual conviction was a stark reminder that we are still far too reliant on the courage of brave women who choose to come forward despite knowing they will pay a heavy price and may not be believed – and a handful of persistent journalists who risk everything to tell their stories.
"Women must feel safe in their jobs, whistleblowers must be protected, and those who abuse their position must no longer be able to hide behind it."

articles.title_orig: Garcia lists Wiles among 4 former officials facing congressional probes
articles.title_zh: Garcia lists Wiles among 4 former officials facing congressional probes
articles.content_orig:
House Democrats are preparing a wave of investigations into the Trump administration, with former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles among those facing scrutiny, a top lawmaker said Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., said congressional committees plan to examine recent allegations regarding whether Wiles engaged in lobbying or donor-related discussions tied to administration policy.
“We’re already looking at Susie Wiles,” Garcia said when asked if the committee plans to call her to testify. “With all of this new information that’s come out, it is incredibly serious. And so it’s not just going to be oversight, but I think you’re going to see some action from some other committees.”
Garcia said the inquiries will not stop with current officials, warning that several former aides and political allies remain on lawmakers’ radar.
“Just because you’re no longer in the administration and whether your name is Susie Wiles, whether it’s Kimberly Guilfoyle, whether it is Corey Lewandowski, whether it is Kristi Noem, you are being investigated and there needs to be accountability in that space,” Garcia said.
The California Democrat pointed to earlier controversies, including administration discussions involving Vice President JD Vance regarding the federal handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case and Ghislaine Maxwell, as part of the broader review.
When asked how incoming House leaders expect to balance oversight battles with routine governing, Garcia acknowledged that cooperation with the White House will be difficult. He said Democrats intend to introduce legislation targeting consumer costs, including fuel and groceries, while pressing forward with committee probes.
“We’re going to put bills in front of the president on affordability starting day one,” Garcia said. “So we’ll have to see if he’s serious, but I don’t trust Donald Trump for a second. We’ve got to be focused like laser-focused on both the affordability question, but also oversight and accountability.”
Garcia also addressed newly introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. While he criticized the policy records of other cabinet leaders, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Garcia said lawmakers are directing their immediate impeachment efforts toward Hegseth.
“Right now the complete focus needs to be on Pete Hegseth,” Garcia said, adding that he expects a close vote when the resolution moves forward.

The U.S. stock market will be open for regular trading hours on Wednesday, November 11, 2026 . While Veterans Day is an official federal holiday that halts mail delivery and closes government offices and commercial bank lobbies nationwide, major American stock exchanges do not observe the holiday.
However, the financial sector operates under a split schedule on November 11: while equity markets run at full capacity, fixed-income bond markets and the Federal Reserve payments system will be closed.
Both primary American equity exchanges will conduct business as usual on Wednesday:
Although extended-hours trading will be available, market analysts note that overall equity trading volume could be lighter than usual due to the closure of institutional banking and credit channels.
Unlike the stock market, the U.S. fixed-income market follows the holiday calendar set by the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (SIFMA):
Traders participating in global and decentralized assets will encounter no holiday interruptions:

articles.title_orig: Chip stocks' slide nears $5 trillion as Nvidia hits most extreme selling level since 2019
articles.title_zh: Chip stocks' slide nears $5 trillion as Nvidia hits most extreme selling level since 2019
articles.content_orig:
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
"Markets bottom on bad news," is one of those smart-sounding rules of thumb that proves true just often enough to remain a Wall Street cliché in good standing.
Did the brutal weeks-long punishment of AI stocks culminate last week and reverse higher Monday after a pileup of adverse headlines? In the past week, American voters resoundingly opposed data-center construction across much of the country and Anthropic lowered its target IPO valuation just before a sex-and-espionage scandal struck the one-man embodiment of the entire AI economy, Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
The story of a market taking a cue from a crescendo of bad news after a nasty setback to stage a resounding bounce holds together well enough for now, after Monday's 3.4% jump in the Nasdaq-100 and 7% rip in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), even as Nvidia shed 4.3%.
Based purely on the tactical evidence, the tech-hardware complex came into the week pretty well washed out and primed to bounce. Numerous trading desks reported historically rare intensity of net selling in the group by institutions into last Thursday's risk purge. The Nasdaq-100 was as oversold on several metrics as it had been at the March 30 Iran-selloff low. The CBOE S&P 500 Volatility Index has put in a nice spike of the sort usually associated with a passing storm, shooting up to 28 and then receding below 20.
The recent dump in the Nasdaq and uptick in risk aversion, "had many elements of capitulation," says Laurent Laskowski, options strategist at Baird Strategas: "record options activity, a sharp spike in volatility, skew and correlations, an inverted VIX curve, and forced liquidations…The setup, therefore, is one where the market is seeing the [downside] left tail narrowing while the [upside] right tail is fattening."
Several technical-analysis gurus (including Macro Risk Advisors' John Kolovos, whose work is cited below) argue the market hasn't quite served up a "fat pitch" to buy the pullback aggressively. Maybe so. But FanGraphs calculates that in Major League Baseball only about 7% of all pitches are in the very center of the strike zone. While those fat pitches result in some 23% of all home runs hit, the other three-quarters of balls that fly over the wall come with less-perfect setups around the edges of the zone.
I wouldn't argue too strenuously against this tech-centered rally carrying on for a bit, for these reasons as well as the fact that valuations have become far less demanding. Last week, I noted Big Tech had not to that point responded to moderately stressed conditions but was getting closer, and "the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market." Monday's blip higher could be a start, with plenty still to prove.
But this AI-driven part of the market has lately shown itself less worthy of investor trust, leaving enough hints of structural damage to the bull case that faith can't be restored right away.
In a late-June column , I asked, "Was May 14 a consequential moment for this market, at least tactically?" That date, nearly six months ago, was when the S&P 500 spurted higher to reach the 7500 level for the first time; the index has never reached escape velocity since and in fact crossed above 7500 again just yesterday.
May 14 was when highly touted AI-chip upstart Cerebras came public and its shares more than doubled to a high of $386, as President Trump and China's leader were reported to have made progress on ending the Iran war. Since then, Cerebras has collapsed to $97, the semiconductor group is off 17% and the Iran conflict continues.
A month later the SpaceX IPO was another apparent culmination of New Era tech enthusiasm; it might not have been an important peak in AI excitement, but if it were the market action since would possibly resemble what we've seen since.
Perhaps a half-year reckoning period during which the market has refused to pay up for 30% annual earnings growth for two straight quarters is enough to build a new base constructed on more modest expectations. I've been focused on late-cycle tremors unsettling markets in the form of peak earnings growth, peak capex, peak index concentration, a tighter Federal Reserve and credit flareups. This all explains the market's multi-month stall, and they remain.
But it's important to remain open to the chance that these could end up amounting to mere mid-cycle turbulence, as Morgan Stanley chief investment officer Mike Wilson has been arguing .
First, though, the tape will need to show more progress than a nice, broad single-day comeback. Another rule of thumb holds that a rebound rally needs at least to carry above the 20-day moving average to prove that it's not merely a reflexive dead-cat bounce. This would require a 1.3% gain from Monday's close for the S&P 500, 3.7% for the Nasdaq-100 and 9% for the SOX.
Without pretending any clear sense of what the various Nvidia investigations will mean for its China sales, leadership or long-term earnings power, we can say for sure that the scandal arrived at a fairly opportune time for the market.
Valuations have been pounded to multi-year lows on persistent worry that current profits are unsustainable and the group remains vulnerable to any slowdown in data-center builds. This allowed, for a day, every other semiconductor stock to whistle higher as Nvidia lost some $200 billion in market cap on a blistering $80 billion in dollar-volume traded in the stock.
The S&P 500 as a whole, of course, has grown optically cheaper, too, with semis bolstering the projected earnings and investors declining to give the group credit for their sustainability.
The issue remains that less of those earnings are set to manifest as free cash flow as the hyperscalers spend manically. As this chart comparing the valuation gauges shows, the market looks a good deal less cheap on free cash flow than earnings.
A proper bull case for the market from here might be that the likes of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft will resume harvesting free cash flow, on which investors might place a higher multiple than they're willing to bestow on those hot but hard-to-trust chip makers. Not yet a provable argument.
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "While sentiment is dire, our concern is that technology is in a 'bad oversold' condition, where seductive bounces fail to produce lasting lows. Instead, the broader equity market may need to follow technology lower, with a more widespread capitulation ultimately needed to wash out weak hands and establish a durable bottom."
-This enjoyable and illuminating review in the New Yorker of James Gleick's "The Telephone: A New History" inevitably summons parallels between the advent of telecommunications and the current AI buildout. Huge privately financed infrastructure buildout, destabilizing new habits of interaction with technology and constant calls for government regulation in exchange for near-monopoly power. The book cites an AT&T ad from 1909 calling telephones "tools of 'civilization . . . one of the most powerful influences for broadening human intelligence.'"
-Moody's Analytics economist Mark Zandi has a helpful thread suggesting AI is so far adding more jobs than it's costing the U.S. economy. The main reasons are sobering though, with most gains coming from data-center construction and wealth creation for those who own AI-dependent stocks. Cold comfort for information-economy job seekers.
-Last week's election triggering a Democratic takeover of Congress brought comparisons to the 1994 "Contract with America" Republican sweep for its magnitude and message. That election, in Bill Clinton's first term, highlighted deep societal fissures and economic instability.

articles.title_orig: Credit card debt hits record high as Americans struggle with cost-of-living
articles.title_zh: Credit card debt hits record high as Americans struggle with cost-of-living
articles.content_orig:
Americans are increasingly turning to credit cards as financial pressures mount, new reports show.
Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest household debt report , released Tuesday. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier.
Total household debt, including mortgages , auto loans and student loans , also expanded by $334 billion for the July-to-September period to a record $19.1 trillion.
"Overall debt has been growing," the New York Fed researchers said on a press call Tuesday. "This does reflect financial hardship out there."
The average credit card balance per consumer now stands at $6,678, up 2.4% year over year, a separate quarterly credit industry insights report from TransUnion found. The number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million from 174.8 million.
Consumers often turn to credit cards in part because they are more accessible than other types of loans — even though the average interest rate on a new credit card offer is about 24%, according to data from LendingTree . Credit card APRs vary depending on the type of card, the issuer and the borrower's creditworthiness.
"Credit cards continue to be one of the most expensive ways to borrow," said Charlie Wise, TransUnion's senior vice president of global research and consulting.
Over time, an increasing share of new credit cards has gone to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and "those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress," the New York Fed researchers said in a corresponding blog post .
Credit card issuers loosened their lending standards during the Covid pandemic, and delinquency rates rose in the years that followed, the New York Fed researchers said on the press call.
"Macroeconomic headwinds — namely high inflation and rising borrowing costs — have squeezed consumers, with inflation outpacing wage growth for low-income brackets," according to the New York Fed.
Meanwhile, the cost of living continues to climb, with Americans paying more for essentials such as groceries and gas.
Stubborn inflation has now stretched on for years, putting many households in an affordability squeeze. Costs for goods and services rose more than expected again in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics also reported Tuesday.
"Higher prices and higher rates have pushed more people into debt," said Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency.
Balances have continued to swell in the wake of the pandemic, and even though the growth rate is now slowing, "from a household finance standpoint, a lot of damage has been done," Rossman said.
The reports come on the heels of the Democrats' strong midterm results, when many voters expressed their dissatisfaction with the U.S. economy , according to Kyle Moore, chief economist at the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation.
"The throughline connecting so many of Tuesday's outcomes was a recognition that the American economy is failing American families," Moore said, referring to Election Day.

articles.title_orig: Mojtaba Khamenei aide's chilling '40 years' warning surfaces amid US push for Iran deal
articles.title_zh: Mojtaba Khamenei aide's chilling '40 years' warning surfaces amid US push for Iran deal
articles.content_orig:
Fox News senior strategic analyst Ret. Gen. Jack Keane discusses reports that Vice President JD Vance contacted an Iranian hard-liner at President Donald Trump’s direction. Keane argues that Iran is not serious about reaching a deal and would not comply with one.
Iran's top security official, who reportedly received a letter from Vice President JD Vance about resuming peace talks, warned in a resurfaced interview that wartime negotiations with Tehran could drag on for decades, and during which both sides should "be prepared to fight."
Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), now serves as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and acts as a key aide to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. He also helped shape Tehran's military strategy during the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq War .
That eight-year conflict ended after Iran's then-supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, accepted a U.N.-brokered cease-fire that he famously likened to drinking from a "poisoned chalice."
JD VANCE RETURNS TO WASHINGTON AFTER 16 HOURS OF IRAN PEACE TALKS COLLAPSE IN PAKISTAN
Senior Iranian general Mohsen Rezaei issues a direct threat against President Donald Trump as the U.S. repositions aircraft carrier amid rising tensions with Tehran, according to reports. (Ayoub Ghaderi/YJC/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS)
"Ceasefire means an unfinished war," Rezaei had said of the war in a 2006 interview with the Iranian publication Baztab. An English translation of the interview is preserved by George Washington University's National Security Archive .
Asked whether both sides would remain in their positions and begin talks, Rezaei replied: "Yes. Negotiations can take 30 to 40 years and during that time Iran and Iraq should be prepared to fight."
Two decades after suggesting negotiations could drag on for years, Washington has reportedly been seeking talks with Rezaei, a key power player in Iran’s current military leadership.
Vance sent him a letter proposing renewed peace talks between the United States and Iran in October, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Iran said it had received a letter from Vance but had not responded, according to Iranian state media. The semi-official Tasnim News Agency said Iran was awaiting U.S. compliance with its conditions, warning that "any position that contradicts this framework is unacceptable."
TRUMP SAYS IRAN DEAL ‘LARGELY NEGOTIATED’ AS 84-DAY WAR NEARS POSSIBLE END
In June, President Donald Trump had posted a warning on Truth Social that Iran had taken too long to come to terms and would "pay the price," while on Monday, he also said that Iran wanted a deal but warned that another U.S. strike could be about five times as large as the previous.
"We could knock it out fast, or we could knock it out over a short, not a long period of time," Trump said during a C-SPAN interview on " Washington Journal Primetime ."
"I can tell you that Iran would like to make a deal, and we'll find out whether that'll happen," Trump said of the current timeframe.
Rezaei however, has continued to maintain a defiant stance toward Washington, writing on X on Nov. 9: "The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government," he wrote before adding that "Washington flails like a desperate gambler."
"FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.
"Stop denying the West Asian NEW ORDER. Time to SURRENDER to the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out," he said.
Following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, Rezaei also claimed Iran had defeated Washington militarily and politically.
He warned of a "devastating response" to another attack and declared it was time for Washington to "SURRENDER."
RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS NOT 'NECESSARILY POPULAR, BUT NECESSARY'
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) generals and commanders, Mohsen Rezaei (2nd L), Ali Fadavi (3rd L), Ahmad Vahidi (2nd R), and Hassan Hassanzadeh (R) attend a memorial ceremony for IRGC commanders, nuclear scientists, and civilians killed in the Iran-Israel war at the Imam Khomeini Grand Mosque in downtown Tehran, Iran, on July 2, 2025. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Rezaei also rejected reports of ongoing U.S.-Iran negotiations or any planned meeting in Qatar , accusing Washington of spreading false claims to ease economic pressure and lower oil prices. He reiterated that Tehran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its seven conditions were met.
Rezaei has spent more than four decades in Iran's defense establishment. He commanded the IRGC from 1981 to 1997, overseeing operations during the Iran-Iraq War.
In the 2006 Baztab interview, Rezaei also detailed how Iranian leaders distinguished their public rhetoric from military strategy.
Although Khomeini and other Iranian officials called for "fighting till Saddam is toppled" and "until the nuisance is eradicated," Rezaei said Tehran's actual strategy was "fighting up to a victory."
At the time, Iran's battlefield gains, he suggested, were meant to strengthen Tehran's negotiating position rather than achieve total conquest.
IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES
Commanders and members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps meet with Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran, Iran, on Aug. 17, 2023. (Office of the Iranian Supreme Leader/WANA (West Asia News Agency)/Reuters)
"The world did not pay attention to the slogans," Rezaei said in the interview, adding that foreign governments and intelligence agencies focused on Iranian leaders' actions and diplomatic positions.
Rezaei also said Iran had struggled to turn battlefield gains into diplomatic victories because it lacked international alliances and influence at the United Nations.
Rezaei has since faced U.S. sanctions and international scrutiny. The Trump administration first sanctioned him Jan. 10, 2020, under an executive order targeting senior Iranian officials appointed by the supreme leader.
Rezaei had also been accused of involvement in the July 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people.

Interpol approved an Argentine request for a Red Notice against Rezaei in 2007 in connection with the bombing.

articles.title_orig: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.
Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.
The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.
Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.
The revelations knocked about $250bn (Â£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.
According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.
Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.
The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.
The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.
Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.
Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.
The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.
At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.
"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.
He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".
Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.
The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.
Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.
A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".
Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.
Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.
Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.
It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.
Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

articles.title_zh: More H9N2 avian flu cases confirmed in China
articles.content_orig:
Hong Kong’s Centre for Health Protection (CHP) reported two new H9N2 avian flu cases today in kids, including a 9-year-old girl in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region and a 7-year-old boy from Liaoning province.
The girl reported symptom onset on October 13, and the boy on September 20. Mainland China has now recorded 23 H9N2 cases in the past six months. Of those cases, all but six occurred in children.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has tracked 189 cases of human infection with H9N2 since 2015, including two deaths in patients with underlying health conditions. Most cases are mild to moderate in severity, with people typically exposed to infected poultry in their homes of communities.
“Current evidence indicates that H9N2 viruses have not acquired the ability for sustained human-to-human transmission, and the risk of further community-level spread remains low,” the WHO said.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said yesterday that a multistate outbreak of Escherichia coli and Salmonella infections linked to tainted alfalfa sprouts is now over, after sickening at least 77 people.
The case count represents one new infection since the most recent update on October 1. Of the 77 case-patients , three were sickened with both pathogens, 10 with Salmonella , and 64 with E coli .
Cases were reported in 16 states, and six patients were hospitalized for their illnesses. No deaths were reported. Illness onset ranged from May 31 to October 16 of this year.
“The true number of sick people in this outbreak was likely much higher than the number reported, and this outbreak may not have been limited to the states with known illnesses,” the CDC said.
PulseNet first identified this outbreak in July 2026, and in August, Everything Sprouts, LLC recalled certain lots of sprouts sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands at retailers and grocery stores, according to the CDC.
In addition to alfalfa sprouts, radish sprouts and alfalfa sprout seeds were also eventually recalled. Some cases occurred in clusters, with Minnesota and Wisconsin reporting the most cases with 29 and 27, respectively.
At least 8 people in the US have died from measles complications this year; the CDC has confirmed just 4.
Jessica Richman’s daughter Cayden died of influenza at age 3. Flu vaccination may have saved her other daughter’s life.
If replicated in clinical trials, the observational findings could inform ways to prevent the lingering consequences of infection.
People with a reported penicillin allergy are often prescribed clindamycin, an antibiotic with a black box warning because of its high risk of causing life-threatening bowel infections.
A large unvaccinated population plus waning herd immunity created the perfect conditions for the virus to infect adults.
Nearly 6 decades of data show that the epidemiologic landscape has diversified to include respiratory viruses and other emerging pathogens.
The patient who died had contact with infected dairy cattle and had underlying health conditions.
Hillsborough County is the epicenter of the outbreak.

articles.title_orig: November Pixel Drop brings big changes and finally makes HiLight more useful
articles.title_zh: November Pixel Drop brings big changes and finally makes HiLight more useful
articles.content_orig:
Google just announced the November Pixel Drop and as you can imagine, it's a pretty big deal. It introduces a ton of new features , while also making some massive improvements to the overall Pixel experience. Or as Google likes to put it, "new and expanded features make your Pixel devices more personalized, intuitive, and handy." The update starts rolling out today, and it will continue to roll out over the next few weeks. That said, let's dive into everything that's new.
Perhaps one of the biggest additions with the November Pixel Drop is that Gemini Intelligence is going to arrive to more phones. The two highlighted by Google are the Pixel 10 and Motorola Signature 27 . This has been one of the better features to make its debut this year, with Rambler being the highlight .
Going forward, your voice will be more powerful when using it to create a message. No longer will Android transcribe every single sound you make. It will make intelligent choices to filter out the nonsense and pauses. To be frank, Rambler is quite a step up from previous models that really couldn't get the job done.
Users will now have the option to create widgets that are personal to their own needs. We got a preview of this just a couple of months back, with the customizable widget first making its debut on Googlebooks. You will now be able to make these on Android phones.
You can spend all the time you want customizing the widget, and this feature will even eventually roll out to the Pixel Watch 5 and Pixel Watch 4. Summaries for long conversations is rolling out the two wearables as well. Along with with Gemini taking over Call Screen to give you a better experience.
This feature will also be available on Pixel, providing a new barrier between you and an unknown caller. Gemini will take care of asking all the right questions while you can screen the call to see if it matters to you. If it's not too pressing, Gemini will take down all the information, or if you want to hop in, you can jump into the call to take over.
Custom Icons are now getting a small boost, with Google adding more styles. If you would like to change the look of your phone , you're now going to have more options. It's not for everyone, but we recommend trying it out at least once.
It's not a huge update, but older Pixel phones will now get a universal search feature that will allow them to search for whatever they are looking for with just one search. It's easy and convenient. This change will apply to the Pixel 6 and newer devices.
I think we can all agree that Google HiLight was a huge disappointment. There was so much expectation from the notification light that it really fell flat when it didn't even deliver on the basics.
Even two months out from its release , it still hadn't seen any improvements, being dubbed the "most useless Pixel feature ever." Well, today that all changes because Google is allowing one more app to activate HiLight and allow it to come alive.
Going forward, Google Messages will now be supported , with the notification LED showing off a glow when you receive a message from a favorite contact. Now, we know that isn't the biggest update, but at least it's something.
If you're willing to do a little work, you can always take control and customize HiLight to your liking . It will be interesting to see how far Google will take HiLight or if it's just something that will fade away.
Not every update has to hit a home run out of the park, but we do like to see improvements that make the daily experience just a touch better. Google has delivered with its Pixel updates this year, especially with Android 17.
The major OS update even revitalized older Pixel devices, making them feel brand new again . It's been a pretty good year for Pixel owners, we can't wait to see what Google has in store for 2027.

articles.title_orig: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
articles.title_zh: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
articles.content_orig:
The victory comes after an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones
A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.
London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."
The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."
Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.
It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.
Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.
Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.
The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.
Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.
The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.
Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".
Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.
"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."
Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

articles.title_orig: Bonds Tumble as Hot Inflation Fuels Bets on More Fed Rate Hikes
articles.title_zh: Bonds Tumble as Hot Inflation Fuels Bets on More Fed Rate Hikes
articles.content_orig:
US Treasuries slumped, pushing yields sharply higher, after hotter-than-expected inflation data and comments from a key Federal Reserve official fueled bets that the central bank would need to deliver more aggressive interest rate hikes to cool inflation.
The two-year Treasury yield, which closely tracks expectations for Fed policy, surged 17 basis points on Tuesday. The two-year yield saw its biggest single-day jump since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s unveiling of tariffs rocked financial markets.
The rocky day for bonds started after Fed Governor Chris Waller said during remarks in London that he would consider backing a jumbo rate hike of 50 basis points (a half point) at the US central bank’s December policy meeting if core inflation – a measure that strips out the volatile categories of food and energy – continues to come in at 0.3% or higher.
“Then, a stronger policy move may be needed,” he said. “Hiking only 25 basis points [a quarter point] would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.”
US inflation rose more than expected last month
Waller said he wants to monitor how the AI buildout is impacting prices of high-tech goods, and if the rise in energy prices this year is continuing to add to inflationary pressures. Oil prices have dropped in recent days, but remain well-above their pre-Iran war levels.
Consumer price data released Tuesday showed core inflation rose 0.3% from a month earlier, more than the 0.2% increase economists had expected. Yields surged higher after the data release.
The key 10-year Treasury yield jumped 10 basis points to 4.98% and briefly rose above 5% during trading. The 10-year yield influences the cost of borrowing across the economy, most notably mortgage rates.
An auction of 10-year notes on Tuesday saw soft demand, according to market strategist Peter Boockvar, adding to pressure on bonds.
Meanwhile, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said in remarks in Houston on Tuesday that the Fed needs to deliver at least two additional quarter-point rate increases.
“The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment,” Logan said. “It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Fed] has moved so far this fall.”
Traders are now pricing in a 91% chance of a quarter-point rate hike and a 9% chance of a half-point rate hike in December, according to CME FedWatch. Just one week ago, traders were pricing in a 77% chance of a quarter-point hike and a 23% chance of the Fed holding rates steady.
“October’s economic data profile and a hawkish shift in Fed-speak have prompted the market to reassess whether a faster pace of Fed policy tightening may be warranted,” Vail Hartman, US rates strategist at BMO Capital Markets, wrote in a note.
Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander, said in a note that he remains convinced the Fed will hike rates by 25 basis points in December, adding that Waller’s consideration of 50 basis points likely doesn’t represent the consensus view among Fed officials.
“Having said that, I would also note that if the inflation data do not show signs of improvement in the coming months, then my expectation of no further tightening in 2027 is in jeopardy,” Stanley wrote.
Stocks closed slightly lower Tuesday. The S&P 500 was down 0.4% and the Nasdaq ticked down by 0.74%. Nvidia shares fell 5.47%, extending a recent bout of weakness over concerns about the board’s investigation into reports CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Nvidia shares closed at their lowest level since March 30.

articles.content_orig:
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe .
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.
Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom given it is the sole manufacturer of a crucial computer chip required for successfully operating AI tools.
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials keen to win the AI race.
Alice Huang was an executive at a Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.
The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.
Nvidia has also maintained the US government did not inform the firm that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.
According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring of this year warning that the Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Beijing has rejected claims that Jensen Huang has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".
US President Donald Trump said Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the Nvidia boss told him "I had no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed the him.
However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Jensen Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.
The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC.
The committee has the authority to subpoena Jensen Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before the committee, if deemed necessary.
When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.
Joon Kim, who will lead Nvidia's investigation, is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focused on fraud and other criminal acts.
Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.
The investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with Nvidia.
He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.
It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang.
A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any additional of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

articles.title_orig: All 7 Anthropic founders will each cash out about $250M in IPO
articles.title_zh: All 7 Anthropic founders will each cash out about $250M in IPO
articles.content_orig:
As Anthropic barrels toward an enormous IPO that could value it at $1.4 trillion, the company has disclosed a tidbit in its new S-1 filing about how many shares each of its seven co-founders plan to sell.
Each will sell 3,378,378 shares. Anthropic has floated an unusually broad initial price range of $70 to $78 a share. At the midrange of $74, each founder would take in just shy of $250 million.
At the low end, $70, each would have to settle for pocketing just over $236 million in cash; at the high end, $78, each would take in just under $264 million.
However, in an IPO as eagerly anticipated as this one, companies can often price shares above the initial range.
The S-1 is already hinting at high demand. Board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million worth of shares through his donor-advised fund. Board member Christopher Liddell also wants to buy $3 million worth of shares.
The seven co-founders are Dario Amodei, CEO; Daniela Amodei, president and chair of the board; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer (pictured above); Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, interpretability research lead.
After the sale, each of them will own about 3.2% of the total outstanding Class A shares, the S-1 says, or roughly 22% collectively. That’s not their share of the company overall. Class A is just one of Anthropic’s share classes, and other holders, including Amazon and Google, hold nonvoting Class N shares, so the founders’ stake in the company’s total equity will be considerably smaller. Even still, they, as a group, remain in control of the company. Each will also receive one share of Class F stock, which carries supervoting rights. Collectively, the founders will control 51.1% of the votes, but no single founder will hold significantly more shares or votes than the others.
As is now industry lore, the seven left OpenAI to start Anthropic in 2021 after disagreements with OpenAI’s leadership over how AI should be built. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who held senior research and policy roles at OpenAI, were joined by five fellow OpenAI colleagues in forming a company that has said, very publicly and from the start, that it’s more focused on AI safety than its rivals, including the founders’ former employer.

articles.title_zh: Canada’s Carney to raise election meddling concerns in talks with China’s Xi
articles.content_orig:
A recent public inquiry identified China as ‘the most active perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canada’s democratic institutions’
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that he would stress the importance of “non-interference in our affairs by China” when he meets President Xi Jinping later this month.
A 2025 public inquiry into allegations of election meddling identified China as “the most active perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canada’s democratic institutions”.
Carney confirmed he would meet Xi at the November 18-19 Apec summit and would discuss “many things”, including efforts to broaden bilateral trade.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Huang Gets More Bad News. Cathie Wood Keeps the Faith.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Huang Gets More Bad News. Cathie Wood Keeps the Faith.
articles.content_orig:
Democratic leader Sen. Charles Schumer ripped President Donald Trump on Tuesday for defending embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the expense of U.S. national security.
"The press reports that Trump was briefed more than a year ago that Nvidia's CEO was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and Trump didn't do anything – anything – about it," Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the Senate floor.
"Can you believe that?" said Schumer, the Senate's minority leader.
Schumer's broadside came on the heels of New York Times reports that Trump had been briefed about Huang's extramarital affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — whom U.S. intelligence concluded was a spy for China — and opted not to do anything about it.
Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he only recently learned of the allegations about Alice Huang, and the president commented Monday that he "really" believes Jensen Huang's claim to him directly that he had no idea Alice Huang was a spy.
"One of our most important companies that is involved in national security, and the CEO might be having an affair with a Chinese spy, and Trump did nothing about it," Schumer said Tuesday.
"What a dereliction of duty. He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends," Schumer said. "Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang when he ought to be defending our national security. It's that simple, it's obvious."
Schumer's comments escalated growing bipartisan concern in Congress about the Nvidia CEO, whose company makes advanced chips that power artificial intelligence in the U.S. and China's race to dominate that technology.
Schumer noted that Trump earlier this year invited Huang to join him on a state visit to Beijing, and that he took Huang's advice by granting the People's Republic of China "access to some of our most advanced AI chips."
Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump's controversial White House ballroom project, the Democrat said.
"Despite talking a big game, Trump continues to show a troubling resistance to confront China on AI and to protect American national security," Schumer said. "I've been saying it for years: our cutting-edge AI chips are too valuable to fall into the hands of potential adversaries."
Schumer in his speech called on Republicans to join Democrats in passing several pieces of legislation — the AI OVERWATCH Act, the MATCH Act, and the Chip Security Act — which he said would "cut off China's access to advanced American technology."
"We also need answers on Nvidia's influence campaign and how [it] affected the Trump administration's national security decisions, including the loosening – the loosening – of key export controls," Schumer said. "We need a full accounting for Trump's failure to address foreign espionage in the American tech industry."
CNBC has requested comment from the White House about Schumer's remarks.
The remarks came nearly a week after Democrats won enough Senate and House races nationwide to take majority control of both chambers in January. Schumer hopes to be selected majority leader.
Regardless of which Democrats are tapped to serve as majority leaders in both chambers, the party will have the ability to launch investigations into Nvidia and Huang.
Earlier Tuesday, Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., said on CNBC's " Squawk Box " that Congress needs to "get to the bottom" of Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang.
Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia's limited supply of advanced chips.
And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang.
"If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work because people have to have confidence," Moolenaar said.
"We're dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that's funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea," he said. "And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible."
Congressional scrutiny of Huang's affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday, a day after Nvidia announced it was opening an independent investigation of Jensen Huang's conduct.
Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, raised concerns that the scandal could plague talks over export controls for advanced AI chips. "It's important not to have a personal scandal interfere with the substantive policy discussion about to what degree we should be allowing the export of cutting edge chips to our geopolitical competitors like China," Obernolte told CNBC. "I hope this isn't a distraction because that's a very important conversation that needs to happen."
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., said in a press conference on Monday that "we're going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security"
Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the three Republicans wrote.
Mast said Tuesday he did not know whether Huang had responded to the letter he authored with Moolenar and Crawford demanding the tech CEO brief them. "I can't say that I've heard an answer back yet that," Mast told reporters at the Capitol. Mast then rattled off a list of questions he has for Huang, including where the company has been selling chips, what Megaspeed may have been using them for, who has been remotely accessing Nvidia chips and what information was passed between Huang and the potential spy. "Obviously questions relating to his relationship and what information was or was not passed about anything," Mast said when asked what he wants answered.
Mast said he "can't say it would hurt" to hear from the Commerce Department as well, noting he speaks regularly to the Bureau of Industry and Security. "So that's obviously something that falls directly under Commerce," he said

articles.title_orig: Russia and Ukraine begin U.S.-backed peace talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.title_zh: Russia and Ukraine begin U.S.-backed peace talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.content_orig:
krainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that fresh U.S.-brokered peace talks with Russia were "constructive and quite substantive," offering an encouraging assessment of renewed diplomatic efforts by President Donald Trump's administration to end the war.
The roughly four-hour negotiations in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, marked the first direct trilateral discussions involving Washington, Moscow and Kyiv since February, with representatives agreeing to continue talks Wednesday, Reuters reported.
Zelenskyy specifically identified three areas of substantive discussion: humanitarian measures and prisoner exchanges, long-term security guarantees intended to prevent another Russian invasion, and possible steps toward reducing hostilities.
Although he characterized the discussions positively, Zelenskyy did not announce any agreements or specify whether the sides had narrowed their differences on the central disputes standing in the way of a peace settlement.
"The release of prisoners is a priority," Zelenskyy wrote on X following a briefing from his negotiating team.
"They spoke in detail about the substance of security guarantees for Ukraine and the foundations for ensuring these guarantees function over the long term," he added.
"Real tools are needed to block any recurrence of the war."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Paris, also offered an encouraging assessment, describing the negotiations as "very productive," according to The Associated Press.
But Rubio cautioned that substantial work remained before an agreement could be reached.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff represented Washington in the negotiations, following weeks of preparatory discussions with Russian and Ukrainian officials.
Kushner previously said those contacts had narrowed differences between the two countries, although he did not specify which issues had moved closer to resolution, according to the New York Post.
The Ukrainian delegation was led by Rustem Umerov, head of the country's Foreign Intelligence Service, while Russian presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky headed Moscow's team.
Neither Zelenskyy nor Russian President Vladimir Putin attended.
Despite the positive assessments, major obstacles remain, particularly over territory occupied by Russian forces since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Russia controls approximately one-fifth of Ukraine and demands that Kyiv surrender the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in the eastern Donbas region.
Moscow also wants Ukraine to abandon its NATO ambitions and accept restrictions on its military.
Zelenskyy has rejected those demands, arguing that territorial concessions and military limitations could leave Ukraine vulnerable to another Russian invasion.
According to Reuters, U.S. negotiators believe Zelenskyy and Putin might eventually accept a territorial compromise, although a senior Ukrainian official disputed suggestions that Kyiv would consider such concessions.
Another major disagreement concerns the sequence of steps toward peace.
Ukraine wants an immediate ceasefire followed by negotiations on a comprehensive settlement, while Russia insists that broader security arrangements must be addressed first.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated Moscow's position Tuesday, arguing that a comprehensive European security framework should precede a settlement of the Ukraine conflict, Reuters reported.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has taken the opposite position, saying broader security negotiations should follow a ceasefire.
European governments also want a greater role in shaping any agreement affecting the continent's security.
Rubio said Washington hopes eventually to expand the trilateral negotiations to include European representatives.
The diplomatic initiative comes amid continuing hostilities, with Russian forces striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure as winter approaches.
Overnight attacks hit 10 Ukrainian regions and five major electrical substations, causing power outages and killing two people, Reuters reported.
Ukraine has meanwhile intensified drone attacks against Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure.
Trump expressed optimism Monday, saying Washington was seeing a "very strong inclination" toward ending the war because both countries were exhausted by the fighting.
Zelenskyy said he had instructed his delegation to continue negotiations Wednesday and pursue further discussions with American and European officials in the coming days.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
articles.content_orig:
Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but still has to get enough parties on board
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.
"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.
He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".
Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.
"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."
The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.
One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.
On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government.
Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.
This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".
Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.
The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.
The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.
Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside.
If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.
In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.
